question: Which feature is typical of the lower-deck cargo compartments of an airliner?

options.text: Access only from inside the cabin
Unpressurised and unheated in all cases, on all types

explanation: Lower-deck compartments have fire-resistant sidewalls, ceilings and walkways, are usually pressurised and heated, and typically have fire detection and protection.

question: Which two floor limits does a cargo compartment usually have?

options.text: A pressure limit and a humidity limit
A height limit and a width limit only, no mass limit
A volume limit and a temperature limit only
A floor loading (kg/m²) and a running load (kg/m)

explanation: Compartments are limited both by area loading intensity and by running (linear) load, as well as by the maximum mass for the compartment.

question: What limits apply to a cargo container (unit load device)?

options.text: Its own maximum mass and floor limit
No limits at all, because it locks into the floor
Only the compartment's total mass limit

explanation: Containers are standard sizes that lock into the compartment, and each has its own maximum mass and floor loading limit (mass per unit area).

question: How is palletised cargo restrained?

options.text: It is not restrained; its mass holds it in place

explanation: Cargo on standard pallets is held with cargo nets or straps (strops). The forward area of the forward compartment is often configured for pallets.

question: Where is bulk cargo typically loaded on an airliner?

options.text: Loose, at the rear of the aft hold
Inside standard containers in the forward hold only
On pallets at the cargo door
In the passenger cabin overhead lockers

explanation: Bulk cargo is loosely loaded at the rear of the aft compartment and separated from the containers by a restraining net fixed to the floor, ceiling and sidewalls.

question: How are containers and pallets moved inside a cargo compartment with a power drive system?

options.text: By a crane mounted in the compartment ceiling
By the aircraft's hydraulic landing gear system
By floor power drive units, from a door panel
By the loaders pushing them over fixed rollers only, by hand

explanation: Power drive units in the floor, controlled with a joystick at the door panel, move containers sideways and lengthways in the doorway and lengthways along the compartment, wet or dry.

question: What is the purpose of the guides, stops, locks and tie-down fittings in a cargo compartment?

options.text: To heat the cargo in flight
To measure the mass of each container as it is loaded
To restrain the load in flight

explanation: These fittings give adequate g restraint so containers and pallets cannot move in flight.

question: Why are aircraft floors limited in the load they can carry?

options.text: To keep the CG within limits
Overloading damages panels and speeds up fatigue
To limit the volume of cargo carried
To prevent the cargo from shifting in turbulence

explanation: Excess loads can crease panels and cause indentations and, worse, accelerate structural fatigue that can lead to collapse with little warning.

question: What does the running (linear) load limit protect?
explanation: The running load limit protects the underfloor frames. The area load limit protects the floor panels themselves.

question: How is a running load defined?

options.text: The total load in the compartment
Load per inch or foot of length, any width
The load on each floor beam
The load per square foot of floor

explanation: The running load is the total load permitted in any one inch or foot of the aircraft's length, irrespective of how wide the load is.

question: To give the lowest running load, how should a long item be placed?

options.text: Across the fuselage, parallel to the floor beams under it

explanation: The running load is the mass divided by the fore-and-aft length it covers. Placing the longest dimension along the fuselage (at right angles to the floor beams) spreads it over the most frames.

question: What does the area load limit protect?
explanation: Area load limits (kg/m² or lb/ft²) protect the floor panels; running load limits protect the frames underneath.

question: What are the two kinds of area load intensity?
explanation: The two permissible intensities are uniformly distributed (UD) loads and concentrated loads.

question: A load is within the uniformly distributed (UD) floor limit. Which other limits must still be met?
explanation: A UD-compliant load is still subject to the running load limits and to the individual and cumulative compartment load limits.

question: How may a load more intense than the UD limit be carried?

options.text: It may not be carried at all
Only if the compartment is half empty

explanation: Concentrated loads can be carried if approved load spreaders distribute them over enough area to keep within the floor limits.

question: What is normally used as a standard load spreader?
explanation: Standard load spreaders of 2-inch-thick timber protect the floor from concentrated loads or items with hard or sharp areas.

question: A 600 kg box has a base 12 in long and 24 in wide. The running load limit is 40 kg/in. With the 12 in side fore and aft, what is the running load?

options.text: 2.1 kg/in, which is within the limit
25 kg/in, which is within the limit

explanation: 600 ÷ 12 = 50 kg/in, above the 40 kg/in limit. Turning the box so the 24 in side runs fore and aft gives 600 ÷ 24 = 25 kg/in.

question: A 150 kg box measures 3 ft × 3 ft × 3 ft. What is its running load?
explanation: 150 ÷ 3 ft = 50 kg/ft; ÷ 12 = 4.17 kg/in. Quoting 50 kg/in forgets the feet-to-inches step.

question: The same 150 kg box (3 ft × 3 ft × 3 ft) stands on the floor. What is its load intensity?
explanation: Base area = 3 × 3 = 9 ft²; 150 ÷ 9 = 16.7 kg/ft².

question: A 720 kg item measures 2 ft × 3 ft × 10 ft. The maximum running load is 25 kg/in. Which fore-and-aft length gives a running load above the limit?
explanation: 2 ft = 24 in: 720 ÷ 24 = 30 kg/in (over). 3 ft = 36 in: 20 kg/in. 10 ft = 120 in: 6 kg/in. Only the 2 ft side exceeds the limit.

question: The 720 kg item (2 ft × 3 ft × 10 ft) is to be placed on a floor limited to 60 kg/ft². Which face must it NOT stand on?
explanation: 2 × 3 = 6 ft² gives 120 kg/ft² (over the limit); 2 × 10 = 20 ft² gives 36 kg/ft²; 3 × 10 = 30 ft² gives 24 kg/ft².

question: Which rule gives the maximum running load of an item?

options.text: Load divided by its smallest area
Load multiplied by its shortest length
Load divided by its longest length
Load divided by its shortest length

explanation: Maximum running load = load ÷ shortest length; minimum = load ÷ longest length. Smallest area gives the maximum area intensity.

question: Which rule gives the maximum floor load intensity of an item?

options.text: Load divided by its shortest length
Load multiplied by its smallest face area
Load divided by its smallest face area
Load divided by its largest face area

explanation: The maximum intensity occurs when the item stands on its smallest face; the minimum when it lies on its largest face.

question: A 400 kg machine has a base of 0.5 m². The floor limit is 500 kg/m². What spreader area is needed?
explanation: 400 ÷ 0.5 = 800 kg/m², over the limit. Needed area = 400 ÷ 500 = 0.8 m², so a spreader of at least 0.8 m² (plus its own mass) is required.

question: How many inches are there in one foot, as used in running-load conversions?
explanation: 1 ft = 12 in, so a load in kg/ft is divided by 12 to give kg/in. 25.4 is mm per inch and 30.5 is cm per foot.

question: A floor limit is given as 75 kg/ft². About what is this in kg/m²?
explanation: 1 m² = 10.76 ft², so 75 × 10.76 ≈ 807 kg/m². Dividing instead gives about 7 kg/m².

question: Which orientation gives an item the lowest floor intensity and the lowest running load?

options.text: Standing on its end, across the floor beams
Lying on its largest face, shortest side fore and aft
Standing on its smallest face, shortest side fore and aft
Lying on its largest face, longest side fore and aft

explanation: The largest face spreads the mass over the most area, and the longest side fore and aft spreads it over the most frames.

question: Cargo is placed so that its running load is within limits, but its base exceeds the floor's area intensity. What must be done?

options.text: Use spreaders or a larger face
Move it to the aft hold
Nothing; the running load is the only limit that decides

explanation: Both limits must be met. Turning it onto a larger face or using approved spreaders reduces the area intensity.
